title: Data Architecture and Data Sharing Across Government
objectives: Design data architectures that enable sharing while protecting privacy
Apply UK data classification and handling requirements to architecture decisions
Navigate UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 implications for system design
Evaluate data architecture patterns for government contexts including registers, platforms and APIs
Produce Data Protection Impact Assessments as meaningful design artefacts
whyThisMatters:
Government holds more data about citizens than any other organisation in the country. Tax records, health histories, benefit claims, criminal records, immigration status, driving licences, property ownership. The policy aspiration is that this data should flow between departments to improve services, reduce fraud, and stop citizens having to provide the same information repeatedly. The reality is that most government data sits in departmental silos, locked behind incompatible systems, inconsistent formats, and legal barriers that nobody fully understands.

This matters for solution architects because almost every government service you design will need data from somewhere else. Your Universal Credit system needs earnings data from HMRC. Your border system needs criminal records from the Home Office. Your planning service needs land registry data. Every one of these data flows involves technical architecture decisions, legal constraints, security requirements, and political sensitivities. Get it wrong and you either build a system that cannot access the data it needs, or you build one that shares data it should not.

The National Data Strategy talks about data as a strategic asset. The Technology Code of Practice says to share and reuse. But the Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR impose strict limits on what you can share and why. As a solution architect, you sit at the intersection of these competing pressures. You need to design architectures that make sharing possible where it is lawful and appropriate, while making it impossible where it is not. That requires understanding data architecture as a discipline, not just as a database design exercise.

content.heading: Why Data Architecture Matters More in Government Than Anywhere Else
content.body:
In the private sector, data architecture is important but bounded. A company controls its own data, sets its own policies, and can redesign its data landscape without asking permission from external parties. In government, data architecture is a fundamentally different challenge because the data does not belong to the department that holds it. It belongs to citizens, and it is held under specific legal powers for specific purposes.

This creates constraints that do not exist in commercial contexts. You cannot simply copy a citizen's tax record into a benefits system because it would be convenient. You need a lawful basis under UK GDPR, a data sharing agreement between departments, appropriate security controls, audit trails showing who accessed what and why, and retention policies that delete the data when the purpose is fulfilled. Each of these requirements has architecture implications.

Government data architecture also operates at a scale and complexity that most private sector organisations never encounter. There are hundreds of departments and agencies, thousands of systems, and millions of data records that need to be consistent, accurate, and accessible to the right people at the right time. The systems were built over decades by different teams using different technologies with different data models. There is no single schema, no single source of truth, and no single authority that can mandate consistency.

The consequence is that data architecture in government is as much about governance, policy, and law as it is about technology. A solution architect who thinks data architecture means choosing between PostgreSQL and MongoDB is missing the point entirely. The hard problems are: who owns this data, who can access it, under what legal basis, for how long, and what happens when the citizen asks for it to be deleted.

content.heading: Data as a Shared Asset: The Policy Aspiration vs the Messy Reality
content.body:
The National Data Strategy, published in 2020 and updated since, sets out an ambitious vision for government data. Data should be treated as a strategic asset. It should be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. Departments should share data to improve services and reduce burden on citizens. The Government Data Quality Framework sets standards for how data should be managed. The API-first approach in the Technology Code of Practice encourages departments to expose data through well-designed interfaces.

The reality on the ground is considerably messier. Most departments have data locked in legacy systems that predate the internet. The same person might be identified by a National Insurance number in one system, an NHS number in another, a Unique Taxpayer Reference in a third, and a passport number in a fourth. There is no universal citizen identifier in the UK, which is a deliberate policy choice but creates enormous technical challenges for data sharing.

Data quality varies wildly between systems. Address data is notoriously inconsistent. Names are stored in different formats. Dates use different conventions. Status fields mean different things in different contexts. Before you can share data between systems, you often need to solve fundamental data quality problems that have been accumulating for decades.

The legal landscape adds another layer of complexity. The Data Protection Act 2018 requires a lawful basis for processing personal data. Different departments have different legal powers. A data sharing agreement that works for fraud prevention may not work for service improvement. The legal teams in different departments often interpret the same legislation differently, creating barriers that are legal rather than technical.

As a solution architect, you need to understand this reality rather than pretending it does not exist. Your architecture must work within these constraints, not wish them away. The architects who succeed in government data sharing are the ones who understand the legal and governance landscape as well as the technical one.

content.heading: Data Classification and Handling in Government
content.body:
The UK Government Security Classifications policy defines three levels: OFFICIAL, SECRET, and TOP SECRET. The vast majority of government data, including most personal data about citizens, is classified as OFFICIAL. Within OFFICIAL, there is an additional handling caveat of OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE for data that requires extra care but does not meet the threshold for SECRET.

For solution architects, the classification determines what infrastructure you can use, how data must be transmitted, who can access it, and what happens if it is compromised. OFFICIAL data can be processed on public cloud platforms that meet the required security standards. OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE data can also use public cloud but requires additional access controls, audit logging, and handling procedures. SECRET and above require specialist infrastructure that most solution architects will never work with directly.

The practical implications for data architecture are significant. If your system handles OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE data, you need to ensure that access is restricted to people with a legitimate need, that all access is logged and auditable, that data is encrypted in transit and at rest, and that the hosting environment meets the NCSC cloud security principles. These are not optional extras. They are baseline requirements that shape your architecture from the start.

A common mistake is treating all data in a system at the highest classification of any single field. If your system holds mostly OFFICIAL data but includes one OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE field, you do not necessarily need to treat the entire system as OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE. Good data architecture separates data by classification where practical, applying stronger controls only where they are needed. This reduces cost and complexity while maintaining appropriate protection.

Another common mistake is confusing classification with sensitivity. Personal data about citizens is almost always OFFICIAL, but it is still sensitive in the data protection sense. The classification tells you about the security controls. The data protection legislation tells you about the lawful basis, purpose limitation, and individual rights. Both apply simultaneously and both have architecture implications.

content.heading: Designing for Data Sharing: APIs, Registers and Data Platforms
content.body:
When you need to share data between government systems, you have several architectural approaches available. Each has strengths and weaknesses, and the right choice depends on the volume, frequency, sensitivity, and legal basis of the sharing.

APIs are the preferred approach for real-time, transactional data sharing. One system exposes an API, another system calls it when it needs data. This is clean, auditable, and allows the data owner to maintain control. The Government Digital Service has published API design standards that provide a consistent approach across departments. APIs work well when you need current data on demand, when the volume of requests is manageable, and when both systems can be online simultaneously. They work less well for bulk data transfers, historical analysis, or situations where the consuming system needs to work offline.

Registers were a GDS initiative to create authoritative lists of government data: the list of countries, the list of local authorities, the list of government organisations. The idea was sound: instead of every system maintaining its own copy of reference data, there would be a single canonical source. In practice, the registers programme was scaled back, but the principle remains important. Reference data should have a single authoritative source, and your architecture should consume from that source rather than maintaining local copies that drift out of sync.

Data platforms provide a middle ground between real-time APIs and bulk file transfers. A data platform ingests data from multiple sources, applies quality rules and transformations, and makes the result available for analysis and consumption. Several departments have built internal data platforms, and there are cross-government initiatives to share analytical data. For a solution architect, data platforms are relevant when you need to combine data from multiple sources, when you need historical data for analysis, or when the source systems cannot support the query patterns your service requires.

Event-driven approaches publish data changes as events that consuming systems can subscribe to. This decouples the producer from the consumer and allows multiple systems to react to the same change. In government, this pattern works well for notifications (a benefit claim status changed, a licence was revoked) but requires careful thought about event ordering, replay, and the legal basis for each subscriber receiving the data.

Bulk file transfers remain common in government despite being architecturally unfashionable. HMRC sends bulk data files to DWP. Local authorities submit bulk returns to central departments. The pattern persists because it works for large volumes of periodic data, it does not require both systems to be online simultaneously, and it maps to existing legal and governance frameworks. Do not dismiss it as legacy thinking. Sometimes a well-structured CSV file transferred securely on a schedule is the right answer.

content.heading: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018: Architecture Implications
content.body:
The UK General Data Protection Regulation and the Data Protection Act 2018 are not just legal compliance requirements. They are architecture requirements. The principles they establish directly shape how you design systems that process personal data, which in government means almost every system you will ever work on.

Purpose limitation means you must design systems that use personal data only for the specific purpose it was collected for. Architecturally, this means access controls that restrict which services can see which data, audit logs that record why data was accessed, and clear boundaries between processing activities. You cannot build a single data lake containing everything about a citizen and let any service query it freely. Each access needs a defined purpose and a lawful basis.

Data minimisation means you must collect and retain only the data you actually need. Architecturally, this means designing APIs that return only the fields the consuming service requires, not entire records. It means building systems that do not store data 'just in case' it might be useful later. It means designing data models that separate what is needed from what is merely available.

Storage limitation means you must delete data when you no longer need it. Architecturally, this means building retention policies into your data layer from the start, not bolting them on later. It means designing systems that can identify and delete specific records without corrupting related data. It means handling the complexity of data that has different retention periods for different purposes.

The right to erasure means citizens can ask for their data to be deleted. Architecturally, this means you need to know where all copies of a person's data exist across your system landscape. It means designing for deletion, which is harder than it sounds when data has been replicated, cached, backed up, and logged. It means building processes that can verify deletion has occurred across all systems.

Data Protection by Design and Default is an explicit legal requirement under UK GDPR. It means privacy considerations must be embedded in your architecture from the start, not addressed as an afterthought. For solution architects, this is not optional. It is the law. Your architecture documentation should demonstrate how you have considered and addressed data protection requirements at the design stage.

content.heading: Data Protection Impact Assessments as Design Artefacts
content.body:
A Data Protection Impact Assessment is required by law whenever processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals. In government, where you are routinely processing sensitive personal data at scale, a DPIA is required for almost every significant system. Most architects treat DPIAs as compliance paperwork to be completed after the design is finished. This is backwards. A DPIA done properly is a design artefact that shapes your architecture.

A good DPIA asks questions that directly inform architecture decisions. What personal data are you processing and why? This defines your data model and access controls. Who will have access to the data? This defines your authorisation architecture. How long will you keep the data? This defines your retention and deletion mechanisms. What are the risks to individuals if the data is compromised? This defines your security architecture and encryption approach. How will individuals exercise their rights? This defines your subject access request and erasure processes.

The practical approach is to start the DPIA during the design phase, not after it. As you make architecture decisions about data storage, access, sharing, and retention, document them in the DPIA. As the DPIA identifies risks, feed those back into the architecture as requirements. The DPIA and the architecture design should evolve together, each informing the other.

In government, the Information Commissioner's Office provides guidance on conducting DPIAs, and most departments have a Data Protection Officer who must be consulted. Build this consultation into your design process rather than treating it as a gate at the end. A DPO who is involved early can help you avoid design choices that create legal problems. A DPO who sees the design for the first time at sign-off can only tell you what is wrong, not help you get it right.

The DPIA should be a living document that is updated as the system evolves. If you add a new data sharing arrangement, update the DPIA. If you change your retention policy, update the DPIA. If you add a new category of personal data, update the DPIA. This is not bureaucracy. It is how you maintain a clear record of your data protection decisions and their rationale.

content.heading: Master Data, Reference Data and Data Quality
content.body:
One of the most persistent problems in government data architecture is the absence of agreed master data. Master data is the core business data that is shared across multiple systems: people, organisations, addresses, locations. In a well-governed data landscape, there is a single authoritative source for each master data entity, and all other systems consume from that source. In government, this rarely exists.

Consider something as fundamental as a person's address. The Royal Mail maintains the Postcode Address File. The Ordnance Survey maintains AddressBase. Local authorities maintain their own address records for council tax. HMRC has addresses from self-assessment returns. DWP has addresses from benefit claims. These sources disagree with each other constantly. There is no single 'correct' address for a citizen, because different systems capture addresses at different times, in different formats, with different validation rules.

For a solution architect, this means you cannot assume that data from another system will be clean, consistent, or current. You need to design for data quality problems rather than assuming they will not exist. This means building validation at the point of ingestion, maintaining provenance information (where did this data come from and when), designing reconciliation processes for when sources disagree, and being explicit about which source you treat as authoritative for which purpose.

Reference data is simpler in principle but still problematic in practice. A list of countries should be straightforward, but countries change (South Sudan was created in 2011), names are disputed (is it Myanmar or Burma?), and different systems need different granularity (does your system need to distinguish between England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, or just use United Kingdom?). Good data architecture identifies reference data dependencies early and establishes a single source for each, even if that source is imperfect.

Data quality is not a one-time fix. It degrades continuously as circumstances change, as users make errors, and as systems drift apart. Your architecture should include mechanisms for monitoring data quality over time: completeness checks, consistency checks between related systems, and feedback loops that allow downstream consumers to report quality issues to upstream sources. Treating data quality as an ongoing operational concern rather than a project deliverable is a sign of mature data architecture.

content.heading: Common Data Architecture Patterns in Government
content.body:
Several data architecture patterns are relevant to government contexts, each with different trade-offs around consistency, autonomy, and complexity.

The data mesh pattern treats data as a product owned by domain teams. Each team is responsible for the quality, availability, and documentation of their data products. A central platform provides the infrastructure (storage, compute, governance tooling) but the data itself is managed by the teams closest to it. This pattern works well in large organisations where centralised data teams become bottlenecks, but it requires significant organisational maturity and investment in self-service tooling. In government, it maps well to the departmental structure where each department owns its domain data, but it requires cross-government agreement on interoperability standards.

The data lake pattern collects raw data from multiple sources into a central store, where it can be queried, transformed, and analysed. This works well for analytical use cases where you need to combine data from multiple sources and explore it in ways that were not anticipated when the source systems were designed. The risk in government is that a data lake becomes a data swamp: a dumping ground for data with no clear ownership, no quality controls, and no retention management. If you build a data lake, invest heavily in cataloguing, lineage tracking, and access controls.

Event sourcing stores every change to data as an immutable event, building current state by replaying the event history. This pattern provides a complete audit trail, supports temporal queries (what was the state at a specific point in time?), and enables different views of the same data for different purposes. In government, where audit and accountability are paramount, event sourcing has natural appeal. The trade-off is complexity: event-sourced systems are harder to build, harder to query for simple current-state lookups, and require careful thought about event schema evolution.

The canonical data model pattern defines a shared data format that all systems translate to and from when exchanging data. This reduces the number of point-to-point transformations from n-squared to n. In government, where dozens of systems need to exchange data about the same entities, a canonical model can dramatically reduce integration complexity. The challenge is getting agreement on the canonical model across departments with different needs and priorities.

No single pattern is correct for all situations. Most government data landscapes will use a combination of patterns: APIs for real-time transactional data, a data platform for analytical workloads, event-driven patterns for notifications and audit, and bulk transfers for periodic reporting. The architect's job is to choose the right pattern for each data flow based on the specific requirements, constraints, and capabilities involved.

workedExample.title: Cross-Government Data Sharing for the Vulnerable Persons Resettlement Scheme
workedExample.context: The Home Office is designing a system to support the resettlement of vulnerable persons arriving in the UK. The system needs to share data with multiple departments: DWP for benefit entitlements, HMRC for tax registration, NHS Digital for healthcare access, local authorities for housing allocation, and the Department for Education for school placements. Each department has different systems, different data models, and different legal bases for processing. The data is highly sensitive, involving vulnerable individuals whose safety could be compromised by inappropriate disclosure. Previous attempts at cross-government data sharing for similar schemes relied on spreadsheets emailed between departments, which was slow, error-prone, and created uncontrolled copies of sensitive personal data.
workedExample.approach:
The Solution Architect designs a hub-and-spoke data sharing architecture with the following key decisions.

First, a central case management system holds the core record for each person, with strict access controls based on role and department. Each department can see only the data fields relevant to their function. DWP sees enough to establish benefit entitlement. The NHS sees enough to register for healthcare. Local authorities see enough to allocate housing. No department sees the complete record.

Second, data sharing is implemented through APIs rather than bulk transfers. Each department exposes an API for receiving referrals and returns status updates through the same channel. This creates an auditable record of every data exchange and eliminates the uncontrolled copies problem.

Third, a Data Protection Impact Assessment is conducted at the design stage, identifying risks specific to this vulnerable population. The DPIA drives several architecture decisions: enhanced audit logging, time-limited data retention with automatic deletion, geographic access restrictions for certain data fields, and a break-glass procedure for emergency access.

Fourth, a data sharing agreement is established with each department before the technical integration is built. The architect works with legal teams to ensure the technical architecture enforces the legal constraints rather than relying on policy alone. If the data sharing agreement says DWP can only see name, date of birth, and National Insurance number, the API returns only those fields. The restriction is technical, not just procedural.

Fifth, reference data (country lists, language codes, local authority identifiers) uses established government sources rather than maintaining local copies. This ensures consistency across all departments working with the same cases.
workedExample.outcome: The system launches supporting 5,000 cases in the first year. Data sharing that previously took weeks via email now happens in real time. No data breaches occur because the architecture enforces access restrictions technically rather than relying on human compliance. The DPIA is cited by the ICO as an example of good practice. When a new department (the Home Office's asylum support team) needs access, the architecture supports adding them without redesigning the system, because the hub-and-spoke pattern and API-based sharing were designed for extensibility.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The most important lesson was that the legal and governance work took longer than the technical work. Getting six departments to agree on data sharing agreements, legal bases, and data handling requirements took eight months. Building the technical platform took four months. Architects who plan only for the technical delivery will consistently underestimate timelines for cross-government data sharing. The second lesson was that designing access controls at the field level rather than the system level was essential for this sensitive population. Coarse-grained access (you can see everything or nothing) would have been simpler to build but would have shared more data than was lawful or necessary.

civilServiceScenario.title: DLUHC Local Authority Data Platform for Housing and Homelessness
civilServiceScenario.background: The Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities needs to understand housing and homelessness patterns across England. Currently, 309 local authorities submit data quarterly via spreadsheet returns in inconsistent formats. The data arrives late, contains errors, and cannot be cross-referenced with other datasets (benefits data from DWP, health data from NHS Digital, employment data from HMRC). A new ministerial priority requires near-real-time visibility of homelessness presentations across the country to enable rapid policy responses. The department wants to build a data platform that ingests data from local authorities, links it with other government datasets, and provides analytical capabilities for policy teams.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You must design a data architecture that collects sensitive personal data from 309 different local authority systems (many of which are legacy), links it with data from other government departments, provides analytical capabilities while protecting individual privacy, and scales from quarterly batch processing to near-real-time ingestion. The local authorities use at least 15 different case management systems from different vendors, with no common data standard.
constraints: 309 local authorities with at least 15 different source systems
No common data standard across local authority systems
Highly sensitive personal data about vulnerable homeless individuals
Must link with DWP, NHS and HMRC data requiring separate legal bases for each
Near-real-time requirement from ministers conflicts with local authority capacity
Budget of 3.5 million for the platform build over two years
Local authorities cannot be compelled to change their systems
Must demonstrate compliance with UK GDPR purpose limitation
Analytical outputs must be anonymised or aggregated for policy use
Individual-level data access must be restricted and audited
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect responsible for designing the data platform architecture. You must balance the ministerial requirement for speed and visibility with the legal requirements for data protection, the practical constraints of 309 different source systems, and the limited budget.
civilServiceScenario.discussion: This scenario forces you to confront the gap between policy aspiration and technical reality. Ministers want real-time data. Local authorities submit quarterly spreadsheets. Bridging that gap requires architectural creativity and honest communication about what is achievable. Consider whether you can define a minimum data standard that local authorities can map to from their existing systems. Consider whether near-real-time means daily rather than truly real-time, and whether that satisfies the policy need. Consider how you handle the linking of data across departments without creating a single database of everything known about homeless individuals. Consider whether aggregated, anonymised data meets the policy need without the privacy risks of individual-level data sharing. The best answer probably involves a phased approach: start with improved batch collection using a common standard, move to daily feeds as local authorities build capability, and provide real-time only for critical indicators. Be honest about what 3.5 million can actually deliver.

practiceArtefact.description: For the DLUHC scenario above, produce an Architecture Decision Record that addresses the question: 'How should we collect data from 309 local authorities with different systems?' The ADR should evaluate at least three options, consider the constraints, and make a clear recommendation with rationale.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Consider the practical constraints: you cannot force local authorities to change their systems, you have limited budget, and you need to move from quarterly to near-daily data collection. Think about what is realistic given that local authorities have varying levels of technical capability. Consider options ranging from a common API standard to a data ingestion platform that handles multiple formats. Be honest about the trade-offs between standardisation (which takes time and cooperation) and accommodation (which is complex but faster to deliver).
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
Architecture Decision Record: Local Authority Data Collection Approach

Status: Proposed

Context: DLUHC needs to collect housing and homelessness data from 309 local authorities. Currently this happens via quarterly spreadsheet returns in inconsistent formats. The target is near-daily collection to support ministerial requirements for timely policy data. Local authorities use at least 15 different case management systems and cannot be compelled to change them. Budget is constrained at 3.5 million total for the platform.

Decision: We will implement a hybrid collection approach combining a standard API specification with a managed file ingestion service.

Options Considered:

Option A: Mandate a standard API that all local authorities must implement. Every local authority builds an API endpoint conforming to our specification. We collect data by calling their APIs on a schedule. Pros: clean, consistent, real-time capable. Cons: requires all 309 authorities to build and maintain an API, which most lack the capability or budget to do. Timeline would be 3-5 years before full coverage. Does not solve the immediate need.

Option B: Build a universal adapter that connects to all 15 vendor systems directly. We build integrations with each vendor's system and pull data directly. Pros: no work required from local authorities. Cons: requires cooperation from 15 vendors, ongoing maintenance as vendors update their systems, and raises data controller questions about who is responsible for the extraction. Cost likely exceeds budget.

Option C: Hybrid approach with a standard data specification and multiple submission channels. We define a common data standard (schema and field definitions) and provide three submission channels: an API for authorities with technical capability, a structured file upload (CSV/JSON conforming to the standard) for authorities with moderate capability, and a web form for authorities with minimal capability. We build an ingestion platform that normalises all three channels into a common internal format.

Decision: Option C.

Rationale: Option C is realistic given the diversity of local authority capability. It provides a migration path (authorities can move from web form to file upload to API as their capability grows) without blocking progress. The common data standard ensures consistency regardless of submission channel. The ingestion platform absorbs the complexity of multiple formats centrally rather than pushing it to 309 individual authorities. The cost is manageable within budget because we build one platform rather than 309 integrations or 15 vendor adapters.

Consequences: We accept that data will not be truly real-time from all authorities initially. Web form submission is inherently manual and will likely remain daily at best. We accept that data quality will vary by submission channel, with API submissions being most reliable and web form submissions requiring more validation. We commit to providing tooling and support to help authorities move up the capability ladder over time. We accept that defining the common data standard will require consultation with local authorities and may take 3-4 months before we can begin building.

Risks: Local authorities may resist even the common standard if it requires significant mapping work. Mitigation: involve local authority representatives in standard design and provide mapping guidance for each major vendor system. The web form channel may become a permanent crutch rather than a stepping stone. Mitigation: set a sunset date and provide active support for migration.

reflectiveQuestions: Think about a system you have worked on that needed data from another department or organisation. What were the biggest barriers to getting that data flowing, and were they technical, legal, or organisational?

How confident are you that you could explain the difference between a lawful basis for processing under UK GDPR and a data sharing agreement to a non-technical stakeholder? If not confident, what would you need to learn?

Consider the data your current system holds. Do you know where every copy of personal data exists, including backups, logs, caches, and analytics systems? If a citizen exercised their right to erasure, could you comply?

When was the last time you reviewed a Data Protection Impact Assessment for a system you were designing? Did it influence your architecture decisions, or was it completed after the design was finished?
Think about reference data in your current system. How many local copies of data exist that could be consumed from a single authoritative source instead? What would it take to make that change?

knowledgeCheck.question: Under UK GDPR, what does 'purpose limitation' mean for data architecture?
options: Data can only be stored in one database per purpose
Personal data must only be used for the specific purpose it was collected for
Each API endpoint can only serve one purpose
Data must be deleted after it has been used once
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Purpose limitation is a core UK GDPR principle requiring that personal data collected for one purpose is not repurposed for something else without a separate lawful basis. For architects, this means designing access controls and data flows that enforce purpose boundaries technically, not just through policy.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary security classification for most personal data held by UK government departments?
options: SECRET
OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE
OFFICIAL
CONFIDENTIAL
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The vast majority of government data, including personal data about citizens, is classified as OFFICIAL. OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE is a handling caveat within OFFICIAL for data requiring extra care. SECRET and TOP SECRET are for national security material. CONFIDENTIAL is not a current UK government classification level.

knowledgeCheck.question: When is a Data Protection Impact Assessment legally required?
options: For every new IT system regardless of whether it processes personal data
Only when processing data classified as SECRET or above
When processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms
Only when sharing data with organisations outside the UK
knowledgeCheck.explanation: UK GDPR Article 35 requires a DPIA when processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals. In government, where systems routinely process sensitive personal data at scale, this threshold is met for most significant systems. The DPIA should be started during design, not completed as an afterthought.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the main advantage of API-based data sharing over bulk file transfers between government departments?
options: APIs are always faster than file transfers
APIs provide real-time access with auditable, controlled data exchange
APIs eliminate the need for data sharing agreements
APIs automatically comply with UK GDPR
knowledgeCheck.explanation: APIs provide real-time, auditable data exchange where the data owner maintains control over what is shared and can log every access. They do not eliminate the need for legal agreements or automatically ensure GDPR compliance, and they are not always faster than bulk transfers for large datasets. Their key advantage is controlled, auditable, granular access.

knowledgeCheck.question: In the context of government data architecture, what problem does a 'canonical data model' solve?
options: It ensures all government systems use the same database technology
It reduces point-to-point integration complexity by providing a shared format for data exchange
It eliminates the need for data quality checks
It provides a single database that all departments share
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A canonical data model defines a common format that systems translate to and from when exchanging data. Without one, connecting n systems requires n-squared unique transformations. With one, each system only needs to translate to and from the canonical format, reducing complexity from n-squared to n. It does not mean a shared database or shared technology.
